title: India's Education Minister Breaks Silence on NEET Crisis, Promises Reforms as Youth Protests Escalate
excerpt: Dharmendra Pradhan's first public response comes after tens of thousands of 'cockroach' movement protesters clashed with police in Delhi and opposition leaders were detained outside PM Modi's residence.
body:
• Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan broke his silence on the NEET crisis, committing to discuss reforms in Parliament — his first remarks since protests began last month
  • Tens of thousands of youth protesters clashed with police in Delhi on Monday, with 180 people injured including 118 police personnel, in the biggest youth challenge to Modi since 2014
  • Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka, and SP chief Akhilesh Yadav were detained outside PM Modi's residence on Tuesday during a sit-in demanding accountability
  • The Cockroach Janta Party movement, born from online satire after India's chief justice called unemployed youth 'cockroaches,' has amassed 22 million Instagram followers

India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has broken weeks of silence on the country's spiraling exam crisis, pledging that the Modi government is "100% committed" to discussing NEET reforms on the floor of Parliament — a significant concession as youth-led protests escalate into the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's third term.

A Crisis That Began With a Leaked Exam

The immediate trigger was the cancellation of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), India's sole gateway to undergraduate medical courses, after question papers were found to have been leaked in May. Roughly 2 million students sat for the exam, which was subsequently scrapped. About a dozen student suicides have been linked to its cancellation, according to local media reports.

The leaks struck a raw nerve in a country where millions of young people spend years cramming for high-stakes entrance exams, competing for fewer than 150,000 medical school seats annually. Exam paper leaks are not uncommon in India, but this one coincided with the birth of the self-named Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical online movement that has channeled youth frustration into real-world action.

"We owe our students more than outrage. We owe them answers, reforms and accountability. That is exactly what our government remains committed to delivering."

— Dharmendra Pradhan, Education Minister

From Satire to Street Protest

The movement traces its origins to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who referred to unemployed youth as "cockroaches." He later said he was misquoted, but the damage was done. Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate in political communication, seized the moment with a post on X: "What if all cockroaches come together?"

Within 24 hours, 50,000 people had signed up. Five days later, the number crossed one million. The Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account ballooned to more than 22 million followers, attracting coverage from the New York Times, CNN, and the BBC.

What began as internet satire erupted on the streets of Delhi this week. On Monday, tens of thousands attempted to march on Parliament. Police imposed prohibitory orders and declared the march unlawful. Tear gas and baton charges followed, injuring an estimated 180 people — 118 police personnel and roughly 60 protesters, according to Delhi Police. Protest leaders say more than 150 demonstrators were hospitalized.

Opposition Enters the Fray

The protests gained a sharply political dimension on Tuesday when Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav staged a sit-in outside the gates of PM Modi's residence demanding accountability.

Police forcibly removed and detained the opposition leaders. Footage of Gandhi lying on the road, resisting as officers tried to lift him, circulated widely. An aide said he suffered an injury below his eye. Priyanka Gandhi was filmed clinging to the door of a police bus as it started moving.

"An attack on students is an attack on every Indian family," Gandhi said before his detention. "PM Modi believes he can get away without answers, without consequences. He cannot. Not this time."

All detained leaders were released later Tuesday evening.

Government Response

Pradhan's response, posted on X late Tuesday, sought to separate the government's commitment to students from the opposition's political maneuvering. "The students of India deserve far better than being treated as props in a political campaign," he wrote.

Earlier that day, Prime Minister Modi made his first remarks on the crisis, telling NDA MPs that "strongest possible steps are being taken to protect the interest of the students" and calling the paper leaks a "grave sin." Health Minister J.P. Nadda also met with CJP delegation leaders but offered no concrete commitments.

What Comes Next

Thousands of protesters remain camped at Jantar Mantar, the traditional protest site in central Delhi, where movement leaders say they will stay until their demands are met. Those demands have widened beyond Pradhan's resignation to include compensation for families of students who died by suicide, the release of fasting activist Sonam Wangchuk, and increasingly, calls for Modi himself to resign.

With state elections approaching in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, opposition parties are maneuvering to position themselves as champions of India's youth. Political analysts note that every major party is now making its own electoral calculations around the movement.

"It's not a political protest," a CJP spokesperson insisted. "It's a movement of the masses, of students. We appreciate the support from the opposition, but we won't let any politics happen here."
image_caption: Protesters from the Cockroach Janta Party gather at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi during demonstrations demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. The youth-led movement has become the biggest public challenge to Prime Minister Modi since he took power in 2014.
nri_angle: The NEET exam crisis and student protests have galvanized Indian diaspora communities worldwide, with solidarity demonstrations in New York, London, and other cities.
author: Diaspora Desk
